title: The Harness Became the Variable: What Changed This Month
question: What changed this month in how AI agent harnesses are built, evaluated, and operated, and which developments matter most to practitioners?
argument: This month's developments converge on one shift: the harness — not the model — is increasingly the measured independent variable. Controlled experiments now show harness design changing solve rates and cost by large margins, evaluation moved from grading trajectories to grading terminal backend state, and vendors shipped orchestration, sandboxing and memory primitives that hand more of the loop-shaping decision to the model itself. The practical consequence is that harness choices are now things you can measure rather than things you argue about.
synthesis:
Three independent strands land in the same place. First, measurement: Martin Fowler's site published a controlled experiment where the same brief was built with and without a behavioral harness across ten runs per condition, and the harness turned a cost-optimized model from 3/10 to 10/10 acceptance while a frontier model passed 10/10 either way — a result the author himself describes as contradicting his expectation. Second, evaluation moved its grading surface: ThinkingBox grades terminal backend database state rather than tool calls, and reports that 67.24% of executable-check failures still terminated cleanly with no tool error — meaning a trajectory-based grader would have scored those runs as fine. Third, vendors shipped primitives that shift where loop-shaping happens: Anthropic's dynamic workflows let Claude write its own orchestration program rather than requiring a developer-configured coordinator and subagent roster; Microsoft Agent Framework shipped CodeAct sandboxing, managed semantic memory, and a hosted-agent isolation model that separates user identity from sandbox session; and Microsoft's own agent-framework blog published a side-by-side architectural comparison of A2A specialists versus distributed skills over MCP with execution traces.

What our analysis adds beyond any single source is the connection between the first two strands. Fowler's result says a harness can substitute for model capability on a specific task. ThinkingBox's result says the signals most harnesses currently use to decide whether work succeeded — clean termination, no tool error — are wrong roughly two thirds of the time on failed runs. Put together: the harness is now a lever worth pulling, but the instrument most teams use to tell whether pulling it helped is miscalibrated. The vendor releases this month supply more levers (self-planned topologies, snapshot sandboxes, semantic memory) without supplying better instruments; the instruments came from research and from practitioner benchmarking, not from the vendors shipping the levers.
limitations: The strongest counterargument is sample size and generality. Fowler's experiment is one greenfield Java service with an unusually detailed brief, ten runs per condition, and the author explicitly flags that he has not tested legacy code, other languages, or vague requirements. ThinkingBox tasks are synthetic reconstructions. The vendor items (Anthropic flows, Microsoft Agent Framework, Foundry isolation, LangChain Managed Deep Agents) are announcements and product documentation with no independent measurement at all — no one outside the vendor has reported on whether flows reduce or increase failure rates, or whether managed memory recall is good. Missing perspectives: open-source maintainers operating these harnesses at scale, security researchers assessing the new self-planning orchestration surface, and non-US builders. Nearly all vendor evidence here is US commercial.

claims.statement: In a controlled ten-run-per-condition experiment, a behavioral harness took a cost-optimized model from 3 of 10 accepted runs to 10 of 10, while a frontier model passed all 10 runs with or without the harness.

locator.quote: A frontier model, GPT-6 Sol, passed every external evaluation either way. But a cost-optimized model, GPT-6 Luna, succeeded in only 3 of 10 unharnessed runs and all 10 with the harness.

claims.statement: The harnessed cost-optimized model reached the same acceptance rate as the unharnessed frontier model at roughly a third less cost per run.

locator.quote: even with the harness overhead, a harnessed Luna attempt cost about 33% less than an unharnessed Sol attempt ($0.273 vs $0.406), and both conditions achieved the same 10-for-10 acceptance rate in this sample.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox grades agents on terminal backend state and reports that about two thirds of its executable-check failures terminated cleanly with no tool error, meaning trajectory-based grading would have missed them.

locator.quote: Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%.

claims.statement: Anthropic announced dynamic workflows, in which Claude itself plans and writes the orchestration program that launches sub-agents, replacing the previous requirement that developers configure a coordinator and a sub-agent roster.

locator.quote: Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work.

claims.statement: Microsoft shipped harness-layer primitives in Agent Framework — managed semantic memory via a Foundry memory provider and Hyperlight-sandboxed CodeAct execution — with an explicit isolation boundary between model-generated code and application tools.

locator.quote: The isolation boundary matters: Hyperlight isolates model-generated code; registered application tools execute in your application’s runtime. Those tools retain their own permissions and responsibilities.
User isolation identifies whose data may be used. At the same time, Foundry hosted session isolation identifies where code and files continue to live.

claims.statement: A single tool-description change, found by inspecting traces rather than scores, eliminated 51 unnecessary skill loads and cut one benchmark run's cost by about 30% with correctness unchanged.

locator.quote: Changing one tool description reduced Codex’s unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and lowered the cost of our benchmark run from $11.85 to $8.34. Correctness stayed unchanged on the benchmark.

claims.statement: A Microsoft practitioner's side-by-side trace comparison found that moving specialist instructions into the orchestrator via MCP skills cut model calls from six or seven to three per request, but consumed roughly 22% more total tokens — fewer calls did not mean less cumulative context.

locator.quote: It did not use fewer total tokens. Across three runs, native skills consumed 13,533 observed tokens versus 11,134 for A2A, about 22% more. Fewer model calls did not mean less cumulative context.

claims.statement: Taken together, this month's measured results show the harness is now a lever that materially changes outcomes, while the completion signals most harnesses rely on are demonstrably unreliable — so the levers arrived ahead of the instruments.

locator.quote: What changes with model capability is not whether independent sensors are needed, but when they run.
A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.
Keep the trace next to the score. The score said pass every time. The tool count and the cost said something was off.

title: Which Claims Held Up: Measured Results, Negative Results, and Numbers Without Methods
question: Which of this month's claims withstand scrutiny, and where are the evidence or interpretations genuinely in tension?
argument: The strongest evidence this month is, notably, negative or conditional: snapshot-based search lost to plain retry, related experience produced no stable transfer, and a harness that helped a cheap model added pure cost to a strong one. Meanwhile the most-shared numbers — vendor throughput and cost claims, decision-model benchmarks, and agent-team gains — arrive without reproducible methods or with explicit null results buried in the detail. The reliable pattern across the month is that results condition on the task and the measurement surface, and sources that report their own negative findings are the ones worth acting on.
synthesis:
Three measured studies this month reported results contrary to their own hypotheses, and that is the signal. The Daytona snapshot paper explicitly states its broad hypothesis was refuted — retry solved 17/25 task-seed pairs against snapshot branching's 6/25 — and then isolates the narrow condition where snapshots do win: when progress lives outside the repository, where full snapshots solved 4/5 and git-diff restoration solved 0/5. MC-EvoBench similarly reports that related experience produced no stable transfer, with all confidence intervals including zero and the single positive contrast driven by one seed. Fowler reports the harness cost his frontier model about seven times more with no detected benefit. Each of these is more informative than a positive vendor number because the authors state the boundary of the claim.

Against that, several widely circulated figures cannot be checked from the retained evidence. The Latent Space roundup carries LangChain's claim that routing to the cheapest adequate model cut median Open SWE cost per task by 64%, Perplexity's claimed 94.5% Decision Bench accuracy, and OpenAI's own 'up to 10x faster' figure — these are reported, not shown. The same roundup also reports a Vals AI result that agent teams cost 1.8–5.1x more with only one configuration improving significantly, which cuts directly against the enthusiasm for multi-agent fan-out that Anthropic's flows announcement encourages. Two pieces of genuine tension are worth naming. First, Arize's tone experiment and the Penn State paper it replicates disagree, and Arize diagnoses the reason: the original prompts confounded tone with brevity instructions, and most of the apparent rudeness saving vanished when only the brevity words were deleted. That is a methodological correction, not a disagreement of opinion. Second, Jellyfish's cross-company telemetry shows cost per merged PR falling 26% and heavy AI spenders gaining most — but the same speaker explicitly says the revert-rate deltas are 'not evidence of a improvement', and the data is observational telemetry from a vendor selling engineering analytics. The honest reading is that the throughput correlation is real and the quality conclusion is not yet supported.
limitations: Every measured result here is a single study with no independent replication: RATED, X-AgentRed, ThinkingBox, MC-EvoBench, the Daytona snapshot work, and Fowler's experiment are each one team's method. The negative results are as un-replicated as the positive ones. The Latent Space roundup is a secondary source summarising vendor claims, so our characterisation of those numbers as unverified reflects what the retained text shows, not an assertion that the underlying methods are bad. Jellyfish and Arize both have commercial incentives in the direction of their findings — Jellyfish sells the telemetry product, Arize sells the eval tooling — though Arize's piece argues against its own first result, which is evidence of good faith. Missing: any enterprise operator publishing independent numbers on these vendor claims, and any security researcher replicating X-AgentRed's red-teaming results.

claims.statement: Full-machine snapshots did decisively beat source-level restoration on a task whose required progress lived outside version control, solving 4 of 5 attempts where git-diff restoration solved 0.

locator.quote: on a custom task whose progress lives in a SQLite database outside git, full snapshots solve 4/5 attempts and source-only restoration solves 0/5

claims.statement: MC-EvoBench found no stable transfer from related experience, with all reported confidence intervals including zero and the single positive result hinging on one seed.

locator.quote: Flows are basically a way to throw test-time compute at hard problems and get more capability faster out of the models

claims.statement: Arize's replication found that most of the apparent token saving from rude prompts was a confound with brevity instructions, not tone, and that accuracy did not move across tones on any model tested.

locator.quote: I ran it again with only the brevity words deleted, against a baseline with no prefix at all, and most of the rudeness discount vanished. Opus’s very rude saving fell from 55% to 15%. GPT-4o’s threatening saving went from 22% to nothing.

claims.statement: The Latent Space roundup reports LangChain's claim of a 64% cut in median Open SWE cost per task and Perplexity's 94.5% Decision Bench accuracy without describing the methods behind either, so both are asserted rather than shown.

locator.quote: LangChain says routing each task to the cheapest adequate model cut median Open SWE cost per task by 64%
Perplexity pplx-decider-v1.1-27b: Claims top Decision Bench accuracy at 94.5% across 1,071 cases, at $0.017 per 1K decisions

claims.statement: An independent evaluation reported in the same roundup found agent teams cost 1.8–5.1x more with only one configuration improving significantly, which sits in tension with the enthusiasm for large-scale sub-agent fan-out.

locator.quote: Results: Teams cost 1.8–5.1x more. Only Sol at medium effort improved significantly, by 7.3 points.
In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also “much more effective at finding all of the details.”

claims.statement: Jellyfish's cross-company telemetry reports a 26% fall in cost per merged PR alongside a 60x rise in AI spend, but the speaker explicitly states the revert-rate deltas are below the noise and not evidence of quality improvement.

A practitioner-run cloning competition found near-saturation among top entrants on its automated business eval while human reviewers ranked the eventual winner 19th, showing that automated graders and human judgement diverge even on the same artifacts.

Across this month's evidence, the claims that survive scrutiny are the ones whose authors state the condition under which they fail — a pattern that separates the research and practitioner reports from the vendor figures.

locator.quote: Snapshotting solves the state-restoration problem, but it does not solve the state-selection problem. Effective environment-level search requires both.

This experiment covered 10 paired runs per model on 1 greenfield Java service, with both models at low reasoning effort. That sample describes the observed outcomes; it cannot establish long-run reliability.

dropped_claims.statement: The Daytona snapshot study explicitly reports that its broad hypothesis was refuted: independent retry solved 17 of 25 task-seed pairs while snapshot-based search solved 6.

MC-EvoBench reports that related experience yields no stable transfer, that the one positive effect is driven by a single seed, and that early execution bottlenecks leave later capabilities unobserved.

title: What To Build Next: Grading Surfaces, Reliability Layers, and the Approval Ladder
question: What do these developments imply for harness builders, and what should they watch next?
argument: The actionable consequence of this month is to change three things in your harness: move your pass/fail signal from trajectory to terminal state, add a reliability layer between tool retrieval and tool execution, and formalise autonomy as a ladder with explicit evidence gates rather than a binary. These are not aspirational; each is supported by a specific measured result or a documented practitioner framework from this window, and together they address the same underlying problem — that an agent's self-report of success is the least trustworthy signal in the system.
synthesis:
Piece 01 established that the harness is now a measurable variable; piece 02 established that most published numbers condition heavily on task and measurement surface. This piece draws the operational conclusion. Start with the grading surface: ThinkingBox's finding that two thirds of failures terminate cleanly means that any production gate keyed on 'the agent said it was done' is systematically blind, and the same source says the fix is available in production, not just in benchmarks. Then the reliability layer: RATED reports that over half of crawled agent tool catalogs exhibit critical flaws, and that re-ranking retrieval candidates on live execution feedback cut fault selection from 86.2% to 2.9% under a 30% failure rate at under 0.2ms added latency — the cheapest intervention in this month's evidence by a wide margin, if the result replicates. Then the permissions layer: X-AgentRed shows that composing benign cross-service tool calls discovers harmful paths at 1.77x the rate of the prior baseline while touching 2.99x as many tools, which means the attack surface grows with your tool catalog, not with your prompt.

Two practitioner talks supply the governance pattern that matches this evidence. Both the Jellyfish-adjacent enterprise talks describe the same four-rung ladder — suggest, draft, act-with-approval, act — and both insist that promotion between rungs requires recorded evidence rather than confidence. Michele Grant's version adds the warning that matters most for harness builders: at the exceptions-only rung, your blind spot is what the agent failed to flag, and a falling override rate can mean the review depth slipped rather than the agent improved. Paden Gayle's version specifies what the log must contain to reconstruct a decision — prompt, model version, configuration, output, reviewer action — which is precisely the record the EU AI Act's six-month retention requirement will demand of high-risk systems from December 2027. What to watch next: whether RATED-style reliability re-ranking shows up in any production MCP client; whether snapshot-based state restoration finds a selection heuristic, which its authors name as the open problem; and whether vendors shipping self-planning orchestration also ship terminal-state verification, or leave that to their customers.
limitations: The strongest counterargument is that the recommendations rest on evidence of very different weight. RATED's 86.2%-to-2.9% figure is a single unreplicated paper using injected failures on a synthetic protocol, not a production deployment; the authors themselves list validating it in live agent runtimes as future work. X-AgentRed's harmful-path rates depend on LLM judges whose disagreement the paper quantifies — accepting either judge raises reported rates by 15 to 30 percentage points versus requiring agreement. The autonomy-ladder talks are case narratives, one explicitly described as illustrative, with no measured outcomes at all. The EU AI Act guidance is vendor-authored by a company selling the tracing product that would satisfy the obligation, and it states plainly that it is engineering guidance, not legal advice. We have no independent enterprise operator confirming any of these patterns at scale, and no security-researcher assessment of whether self-planning orchestration widens the surface X-AgentRed probes.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox argues the terminal-state check it uses for grading is available as a production signal, implying harness builders should verify end state before committing rather than trusting the agent's summary.

locator.quote: The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox attributes roughly four in five failures to tool handling rather than reasoning, framing error recovery as a harness problem before it is a model problem.

locator.quote: The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

claims.statement: RATED reports that over half of tools crawled from four major agent platforms have critical flaws such as broken links and missing authentication, making tool-catalog reliability a first-order harness concern.

locator.quote: As Figure 1 shows, despite rapid growth, over 50% of these tools exhibit critical flaws like broken links and missing authentication. Many tools are functionally similar, so retrieval cannot rely on semantics alone to identify which ones will execute successfully.

claims.statement: RATED reports that re-ranking retrieval candidates on live execution feedback cut fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under a 30% API failure rate while adding under 1ms of latency.

locator.quote: RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference.

claims.statement: X-AgentRed reports discovering harmful cross-service paths at 1.77x the rate of its baseline while covering 2.99x as many distinct tools, indicating that compositional risk scales with the size of the connected tool catalog.

locator.quote: Across four frontier agentic models, X-AgentRed achieves \(1.77\times\) the harmful path rate of STAC and explores a more diverse set of tools, yielding \(2.99\times\) the tool coverage on average.

claims.statement: A practitioner framework for staged autonomy warns that at the exceptions-only rung the main vulnerability is what the agent failed to flag, and that a falling override rate may indicate shallower review rather than a better agent.

A second practitioner account specifies the same four-rung autonomy ladder and names the concrete record needed to reconstruct a consequential decision: prompt, model version, configuration, output, and reviewer action.

Arize argues that EU AI Act high-risk obligations — automatic logging, six months of retention, human oversight, post-market monitoring — are engineering work that largely overlaps with good production agent practice, with a December 2027 deadline.

locator.quote: Most high-risk obligations are engineering work. Automatic logs, six months of retention, human oversight, post-market monitoring, incident handling, and explanations of decisions are things you build. Most of them are already good practice for running agents in production.

claims.statement: The practitioner evidence converges on a single operating principle: the agent's own report of success is the weakest signal in the system, so the harness must supply an independent verification surface at every autonomy rung.

locator.quote: A tool call is not an outcome
A confident final response does not prove the work was completed.

claims.statement: The open problem to watch in environment-level state management is selection, not restoration: the snapshot study names identifying which machine states represent reusable progress as the main unsolved question.

locator.quote: The main open problem is selection: how can we tell when a machine state represents reusable progress rather than a dead end?
